newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Sudan minister delivers message to Kuwait's emir.
newsitem.headline: Sudan minister delivers message to Kuwait's emir.

text.p: A Sudanese minister delivered a message on Wednesday from the African state's president to the emir of Kuwait whose ties with Khartoum were badly strained during the 1990-91 Gulf crisis.

The official Kuwait News Agency (KUNA), which said Sheikh Jaber al-Ahmad al-Sabah received Sudanese foreign minister of state Mustafa Osman Ismail, did not reveal the contents of Omar Hassan al-Bashir's message.
Diplomats said the message, which they believe was the first contact on this level between the two Arab states since the Gulf crisis, heralds the official start of a "slow reconciliation process".
"It is in the interest of Sudan to reconcile with Kuwait, but Kuwait would want the process to be slow and careful, mainly due to domestic reasons," an Arab diplomat said.
Kuwaitis are still angered by memories of what they saw as backing by some Arab states to Iraq during its 1990-91 occupation of their country.
Kuwait had downgraded ties and cut generous financial aid to several Arab states, including Sudan, which it accused of sympathising with Iraq during the occupation.

Ismail, who arrived in Kuwait on Tuesday on the first visit by a Khartoum minister since the Iraqi invasion of the Gulf Arab state, has condemned the invasion and said it was in "violation of international law".

Sudan was among three states which expressed reservations on an Arab League summit resolution in Cairo days after Iraq seized Kuwait. The resolution -- rejected by Iraq, Libya and the Palestine Liberation Organisation -- sanctioned the sending of Arab troops to Saudi Arabia.
The Arab troops later participated in the U.S.-led 1991 Gulf War against Iraq.
Kuwait's government and parliament had discussed in recent weeks in secret sessions the possibility of restoring ties with some Arab states which appeared to back Iraq during the crisis.
Diplomats say such moves might lack public support although there are some within the government who strongly back it.
